title: The First Delivery
passages:
Sára stood in the dim kitchen, the crate empty at her feet and the bell’s low toll still echoing in the stone walls. She lifted the smooth, faceless doll from the wood, feeling the faint heat of the iron straps that had held it shut. The Wheel under the floorboards shivered once more, as if acknowledging the breach of the rule.

She carried the doll across the cold floor to the iron stove, set it gently on the blackened ash, and watched as the faint script on the charred scrap sharpened into clear letters: “Remember.” The bell rang a second time, the Wheel turned a final notch, and the damp tag on the table ceased bleeding ink, its letters freezing in place.

Sára stepped back, the doll now a silent witness on the stove, and the house fell quiet. A fresh tag appeared on the table, its paper still damp, naming her again as a deliverer, but this time the house no longer reached for her memory. She kept the doll, feeling the weight of the paid toll, and waited for the next bell.

The next bell did not come. Instead the mule cart rattled up the causeway in the grey light, and the delivery man stood at the door with his cap in his hands, not crossing the threshold. He would not look at the stove.

"You opened it," he said. It was not a question. "That's on you now. The house doesn't send twice for the same debt."

Sára asked him who had marked the crate. He shook his head. The chalk was already on the wood when the crate came to him at Vaskapu, he said; no hand he saw had made the mark, and his work was to carry and not to ask. Then he set a second, smaller parcel on the table, this one bound in iron, and backed out to his cart without lifting his eyes from the floor.

The tag beside the parcel was damp and already bleeding. It named the place: The Point. It named the deliverer: Ilka Dálnoky. And beneath, in the same cramped hand as the burned ash, a line Sára had not written: *the face is not yours to keep.*

Sára understood then what the house would take. Not her memory this time. The doll wore her sister's face the way a coat is worn, and the house meant to have the face back, to set it on one of the blank things at The Point and leave the wood smooth again. Ilka was to carry it. Ilka, who had lent the skiff, who knew her as Vera, who had left before the bell.

She thought of the woman's shelf of faceless dolls and the child-sized hearthstone. She thought of her sister's smile, gone mid-water, and the word on the ash: *Remember.* Then she lifted the doll from the stove. The wood had gone cool. She wrapped it in her apron, took the iron-bound parcel under her arm, and went out onto the causeway to meet the cart before it could reach The Point without her.
